main_damage_causes: Compression of Vernon's most psychologically complex and sustained scenes (letters campaign, OotP kitchen confrontation, HBP visit) into montages or brief exchanges, stripping the portrait of a man whose fear and pomposity unravel in darkly comic but revealing ways

Removal or softening of Vernon's most explicitly cruel verbal moments — particularly his dismissal of James and Lily's deaths as deserved — which reduces the moral clarity of his antagonism and the emotional stakes for Harry

Loss of Vernon's cunning/scheming dimension (the bedroom bribe, the strategic lying to Harry's face) which in the books prevents him from being a simple buffoon and makes him a more genuinely threatening presence

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (PS) - Vernon's warning at the zoo
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Vernon's warning as calculated cruelty tied to fear and control: he takes Harry aside privately, puts his large purple face right up to Harry's, and threatens no meals for a week if there is any 'funny business.' The threat is personal, menacing, and rooted in his paranoid hostility toward Harry's nature.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Vernon delivers the warning curtly outside the car in a few words ('Any funny business, any at all, and you won't have any meals for a week. Get in.'), framed as a brief parental-sounding caution rather than an act of deliberate intimidation. The physical menace and the close, purple-faced bullying posture from the book are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version emphasises Vernon's calculated, face-to-face intimidation as a defining character beat early in the story. The film flattens it to a throwaway line, slightly softening his deliberate cruelty toward Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (PS) - Vernon's reaction after the zoo / cupboard punishment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book: after Piers identifies Harry as talking to the snake, Vernon waits until Piers is safely gone, then is so angry he can barely speak. He sentences Harry to 'go - cupboard - stay - no meals' before collapsing into a chair, requiring Petunia to fetch him a large brandy. His rage is explosive but also somewhat pathetic and physically overwhelming to himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 shows Vernon physically shove Harry against a wall, grab his hair, snarl at him, then shove him into the cupboard and slam/lock it. The physical assault is added; the near-collapse from rage and the brandy detail (showing his own weakness) are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Vernon is terrifying but also pathetically undone by his own rage — he collapses and needs brandy. The film replaces this with straightforward physical aggression. This shifts Vernon from a buffoon-bully composite toward a simpler physical abuser, losing the darkly comic dimension of his character that the books sustain throughout.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (PS) - Vernon's response to Harry's first letter
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book: Vernon snatches the letter, his face goes from red to green to grayish-white. He reads it, gasps 'P-P-Petunia!', and later goes to Harry in the cupboard to lie ('addressed to you by mistake, I have burned it'), then forces a painful smile and offers Harry Dudley's second bedroom as a bribe — a whole scene of scheming, lying, and attempted manipulation showing Vernon's cunning self-interest alongside his fear.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Vernon snatches the letter and reads it; his face drains of colour. The film cuts quickly. There is no scene of Vernon visiting Harry in the cupboard, lying to his face, or craftily offering the bedroom upgrade as a manipulative bribe. The bedroom move simply happens without the calculated deception scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Vernon is not only fearful and bullying but also scheming and manipulative — he lies directly to Harry and uses a bribe to try to stop the letters. Losing this scene removes a key dimension of his intelligence-within-stupidity: he is cunning when frightened. The film makes him purely reactive.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (PS) - Letters chaos / 'No post on Sunday'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book portrays Vernon's escalating, paranoid campaign against the letters with grim humour and specificity: nailing the letterbox, boarding up the house, sleeping in a sleeping bag at the front door, driving erratically to 'shake them off,' checking into a gloomy hotel. Vernon is shown as a man coming apart at the seams, muttering 'shake 'em off,' humming 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips' while boarding doors, jumping at small noises. His smugness on Sunday ('No post on Sundays — no damn letters today') is a triumphant character beat immediately undercut.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses this into a rapid montage: Vernon rips letters, blocks the letterbox, letters flood in via fireplace, Vernon tries to stop Harry grabbing one, and then announces they're going away. The sustained portrait of Vernon's unravelling paranoia — the hotel, the erratic driving, the sleeping bag at the door, the boarding-up with humming — is largely absent. The Sunday smugness line is present but shorn of the extended build-up that makes it land.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Vernon's obsessive, escalating campaign against the letters is one of his richest comic-yet-chilling characterisation sequences in the books. The sustained portrayal of a man so terrified of magic that he loses all proportion — sleeping on the floor, boarding the house, driving aimlessly — is compressed into a quick montage, significantly reducing the texture of his character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (CoS) - Vernon's 'goodness of our hearts' speech
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book (CoS) establishes Vernon's attitude toward Harry during the summer via the dinner party setup: he is calculating, self-interested, and his 'generosity' is entirely transactional. He never frames keeping Harry as an act of goodness — he is openly hostile and treats Harry as an embarrassing problem to be managed.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 8: Vernon delivers the line 'I should think you'd be more grateful. We raise you since you were a baby, give you food off our table, even let you have Dudley's second bedroom... purely out of the goodness of our hearts.' This is a scripted self-justification Vernon would never offer sincerely — and indeed Dudley immediately undercuts it by noting the real reason. However, Vernon speaking this line at all, framing himself as a benefactor, is a departure from the book's Vernon who never bothers with self-justification to Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but notable: book-Vernon does not present himself to Harry as a benefactor or seek Harry's gratitude in this way. He simply ignores or bullies Harry. The film briefly gives him a self-pitying, self-justifying voice that softens his deliberate indifference into something more like wounded pride.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (PoA) - Aunt Marge inflation / Vernon lets go
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book: when Marge begins to inflate, Vernon seizes one of her feet and tries to pull her back down, nearly being lifted himself, before Ripper bites his leg and he lets go. This is frantic, undignified, and driven by his desperation to maintain control and avoid scandal — consistent with his core characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 13: Vernon initially grips Marge's hands as she rises outside, then as he himself begins to rise, he looks fearfully into her eyes — and deliberately lets go. The film frames this as a conscious choice, and Marge even says 'Vernon. Don't you dare —' before he drops her. This makes Vernon's release a deliberate abandonment of Marge rather than an involuntary loss of grip caused by Ripper.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The distinction is small but meaningful to character: book-Vernon is desperate to fix the situation and is only stopped by Ripper. Film-Vernon makes a conscious choice to save himself, making him more coldly self-serving toward even his own sister. It is a minor tone shift but moves him in a slightly different direction.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 14 (OotP) - Vernon's response to Dementor attack / expulsion letter
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book (OotP): Vernon's response to the Dementor attack and letters is a sustained, complex scene. He initially explodes with rage and tries to throw Harry out ('You're not staying here if some loony's after you... OUT!'). He is genuinely terrified, angry, and confused. The scene includes his struggling to understand Dementors, his grudging partial-comprehension, Petunia's Howler intervention, and ultimately his deflating capitulation when Petunia insists Harry stays. Vernon's emotions arc across the whole scene: rage → bafflement → fear → deflation. His line about the death penalty ('Have they sentenced you to anything? Do your lot have the death penalty?') shows his darkly comic hostility.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 14 drastically compresses this. Vernon briefly accuses Harry ('Happy, are we now? You've finally done it'), reacts to the expulsion letter, and the scene moves quickly to the Order's arrival. The extended kitchen confrontation — Vernon's attempts to understand Dementors, his near-victory in throwing Harry out, Petunia's Howler and her commanding 'He stays,' Vernon's deflation — is almost entirely absent. The death penalty quip is gone. Vernon's complexity in this scene (terrified but also genuinely trying to reason through events in his limited way) is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Vernon's most dramatically rich scenes in the entire series — he almost successfully throws Harry out, is overruled by Petunia, and is shown as genuinely grappling (however clumsily) with a world he cannot understand. The film's compression removes the dynamic between Vernon and Petunia, reduces Vernon's agency in the decision, and loses key characterisation including his darkly comic hostility and his eventual pathetic deflation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene (HBP/implied) - Dumbledore's visit to Privet Drive
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book (HBP): Dumbledore visits number four and the scene is a sustained, pointed confrontation. Vernon attempts rudeness, is smoothly outmanoeuvred by Dumbledore at every turn, has a glass of mead bouncing off his head, and is explicitly told by Dumbledore that he and Petunia failed to treat Harry as a son and inflicted cruelty. Vernon is shown as blustering, impotent, and finally silent under Dumbledore's controlled authority. The scene reveals Vernon's core dynamic — he can bully those weaker than him but is entirely outmatched by genuine authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10 (HBP script) shows Dumbledore arriving, Vernon briefly confrontational ('You will, will you?'), the sofa-knock, the mead glass bouncing on Vernon's head, and Vernon's intimidated silence. The explicit rebuke from Dumbledore about how Harry has been treated ('You have never treated Harry as a son. He has known nothing but neglect and often cruelty') is absent from the film corpus provided, meaning Vernon is not publicly held to account for his treatment of Harry in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's direct rebuke of Vernon is a significant moment of moral accountability — the only time an authority figure explicitly names Vernon's cruelty to Harry's face. Its absence means Vernon is never truly confronted or shamed for his behaviour, which reduces the moral weight of his characterisation across the arc and lets him off the hook narratively.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film (DH Part 1) - Dursleys' departure / Dudley's farewell
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book (DH): the departure scene includes Vernon's cycling indecision, his conspiracy theory about the house, Harry's sharp but weary rebuttals, and — crucially — Dudley's unexpected question ('Why isn't he coming with us?') and his quiet farewell to Harry ('I don't think you're a waste of space'). Vernon's reaction to Dudley's gesture is to freeze in stunned incomprehension. The scene also includes Vernon's attempted handshake that he cannot complete — a moment of stunted, failed human connection that defines the Dursley-Harry relationship's ambiguous close.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene (DH, from corpus): Vernon's conspiracy theory about the house is present; Harry's rebuttals are present. Dudley's farewell moment appears present in the corpus ('Yea but coming from Dudley that's like I love you'). However, Vernon's attempted handshake — his arm swinging up to shake Harry's hand and then being unable to go through with it, closing his fist and swinging it back and forth — is referenced in the book corpus (Scene 883) but this moment of failed human gesture from Vernon is not visible in the film corpus scenes provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Vernon's aborted handshake is a quietly devastating character moment — the closest he ever comes to acknowledging Harry as a human being, and he cannot manage even that. If absent from the film, it removes the only hint of stunted, failed redemption in Vernon's arc and leaves his departure as purely hostile, flattening the complexity of the farewell.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (PS) - Hagrid's hut / Vernon's defiance of Hagrid
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book: at the hut, after Hagrid reveals Harry is a wizard, Vernon finds his voice and delivers a speech of genuine venom: 'I accept there's something strange about you, probably nothing a good beating wouldn't have cured — and as for all this about your parents, well, they were weirdos, no denying it, and the world's better off without them in my opinion — asked for all they got...' This is Vernon at his most nakedly cruel — dismissing James and Lily's murders as deserved, directly to their orphaned son. It provokes Hagrid's furious response with the umbrella.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6/7: Vernon's defiance is compressed into 'He will not be going, I tell you! We swore when we took him in, we'd put a stop to all this rubbish!' and 'I will not pay to have some crackpot old fool teach him magic tricks!' The speech about Harry's parents being 'weirdos' who 'got what they deserved' and the world being better off without them — Vernon's most explicitly cruel line in the entire first book — is absent. Hagrid's threat with the umbrella follows from the Dumbledore insult rather than from Vernon's attack on Harry's dead parents.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Vernon's speech about Harry's parents is arguably his defining moment of cruelty in PS — it reveals the depth of his hatred and justifies Harry's resentment in full. Its removal significantly softens Vernon's characterisation at the story's most important early scene and reduces the emotional weight of Hagrid's protective anger on Harry's behalf.
